newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Overhauling court system is postwar Guatemala need.
newsitem.headline: Overhauling court system is postwar Guatemala need.

text.p: One of Guatemala's biggest challenges once a peace treaty to be signed on Sunday ends 36 years of civil war will be for its wobbly court system to start dispensing justice in the lawless country, analysts say.
"The legal system plays a fundamental role that will determine what happens after the war," Hector Rosada, a sociologist and former government peace negotiator, said.

Reports of human rights abuses have decreased in recent years but real and speedy justice remains scarce for victims, the analysts say. An estimated 140,000 Guatemalans, most of them civilians, died or disappeared in the war, some at the hands of leftist guerrillas but most in army counterinsurgency campaigns.
Only a handful of assassins, torturers and perpetrators of other political crimes from Guatemala's darkest years have been prosecuted, let alone found guilty and sentenced.

The United Nations Mission for Human Rights Verification in Guatemala (MINUGUA) has documented dozens of criminal and human rights investigations and court cases that never get off the ground, are endlessly stalled or are moving at a snail's pace.
Incompetent and terrorised judges, lack of communication between police, prosecutors and the courts, and corruption all weaken the court system, legal observers say.

"The structure of the judicial system is absolutely deficient and it's tied in with the deficiency and corruption of the security forces. You don't know who is more delinquent -- the captured, the capturers or the one who judges," Rosada said.
Perhaps even harder to change is the tradition of untouchability for the army and paramilitary organisations, which has weakened faith in the system.

"Impunity is a blot that has characterised Guatemala's political process under military dictatorships ruled by a national security doctrine," Congressman Amilcar Mendez of the leftist New Guatemala Democratic Front Party said.
He said the court system was "scandalously corrupt" and many judges had received their seats as political gifts, with no thought being given to academic or professional qualifications.

Recent efforts to modernise the system, which still uses handwritten ledgers and hardly any computers, have merely brought confusion. Rules of evidence and trial procedure are being improvised in the courtroom, one lawyer said.

The most widely applauded reform came this year, when Congress did away with a law giving military courts jurisdiction over any crime committed by a member of the armed forces. But the change has not guaranteed that human rights cases move smoothly through the judicial system.

The prosecution of three officers accused of ordering the assassination of sociologist Myrna Mack in 1990 looked hopeful when it was moved to a nonmilitary court, but it appears to have become bogged down in an endless circle of pre-trial moves.
The trial, a litmus test for the courts, set a precedent when a soldier was imprisoned for the fatal stabbing, the first time a member of the armed forces was convicted in a human rights case.
And countless other recent human rights cases have become permanently stuck in the pretrial phase.
